frames.question: Explain how OAuth login works, step by step. I'm adding it to our app.
frames.narration: OAuth can feel like a maze of redirects, but at its heart, it's just a secure way for a user to say 'yes, this app can act on my behalf' without handing over their password. Let's walk through the standard Authorization Code flow, look at the actual token exchange, and check off the security essentials…

tour.say: The core of the process is the Authorization Code flow. It starts with a redirect, gets user consent, and returns a temporary code.

spec.title: OAuth 2.0 Login Flow
spec.sub: The step-by-step authorization code flow for your app.
spec.opener: OAuth can feel like a maze of redirects, but at its heart, it's just a secure way for a user to say 'yes, this app can act on my behalf' without handing over their password. Let's walk through the standard Authorization Code flow, look at the actual token exchange, and check off the security essentials…

props.title: Delegated Authorization, Not Just Login
props.summary: OAuth 2.0 is designed to let a third-party application access resources without exposing user credentials. When used for login, we typically layer OpenID Connect on top to get profile data.

blocks.note: OAuth is about delegation — letting your app get a key to the front door without ever seeing the user's master password.

steps.action: Redirect user to the Identity Provider
steps.detail: Send the user to the provider's authorization endpoint with your client ID, requested scopes, and a redirect URI.
steps.tip: Always include a random 'state' parameter or use PKCE to prevent cross-site request forgery.
steps.check: User sees the provider's login screen

steps.detail: The user authenticates with the provider (e.g., Google or GitHub) and consents to the permissions your app requested.
The provider redirects the user back to your registered Redirect URI, appending a temporary 'code' in the query string.
steps.tip: This code is short-lived, usually expiring in under 10 minutes.
steps.check: Your backend endpoint receives the GET request

steps.action: Exchange code for an Access Token
steps.detail: Your backend makes a secure POST request to the provider's token endpoint, sending the code, client ID, and client secret.
steps.check: Provider returns an access token and ID token

steps.detail: Use the access token in the Authorization header to request the user's profile details from the provider's UserInfo endpoint.
steps.check: You have the user's email and unique ID to log them in

blocks.note: This five-step dance ensures that your client secret is never exposed to the user's browser.

lines.text: Exchange the temporary authorization code for an access token

curl -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \
  -d code=4/0AeaYSH... \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/callback \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code

props.title: Step 4: The Token Exchange Request
props.caption: This POST request must happen strictly server-to-server to protect your client secret.

blocks.note: Your server swaps the temporary code for a bearer token behind the scenes, keeping your client secret completely hidden.

props.title: Handling the Callback in Express
props.footer: Always validate the state parameter before making the token exchange.

blocks.note: In code, the callback route is where you intercept the code, verify the state parameter, and perform the secure POST exchange.

props.recommendation: For user login, always use OpenID Connect (OIDC) so you get a standardized ID token containing the user's profile.

blocks.note: While OAuth handles the permissions, OpenID Connect is what actually gives you the standardized ID token containing the user's profile.

rows.t: Use HTTPS everywhere to protect tokens in transit
Implement PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) even for confidential backends
Strictly validate redirect URIs on the provider dashboard (no wildcards)
Store client secrets securely in environment variables, never in client-side code
Set short expiration times on access tokens and use secure HttpOnly cookies for sessions

props.title: OAuth Security Checklist
props.footer: A single leaked client secret or open redirect can compromise your entire user base.

blocks.note: Security is paramount here — make sure your redirect URIs are strictly matched and your client secrets are never exposed.
The biggest mistake is putting the client secret in a mobile app or frontend code — it must live strictly on your secure server.

frames.question: Compare session cookies and JWTs for keeping users signed in. Focus on tradeoffs, not dogma.
frames.narration: OAuth can feel like a maze of redirects, but at its heart, it's just a secure way for a user to say 'yes, this app can act on my behalf' without handing over their password. Let's walk through the standard Authorization Code flow, look at the actual token exchange, and check off the security essentials.

tour.say: First, let's look at the Authorization Code flow. It starts with a redirect to the identity provider and ends with your backend exchanging a code for tokens.
This is what the actual token exchange request looks like. Notice how the authorization code and code verifier are sent securely from your backend.
Once you have the tokens, you must decide how to keep the user logged in. Session cookies offer instant revocation, while JWTs are stateless.
For storage, avoid LocalStorage due to XSS risks. An HttpOnly, Secure cookie with SameSite protection is the safest place for web apps.

events.title: Redirect to Identity Provider
events.detail: Your app redirects the user to the OAuth server with a code_challenge (for PKCE) and requested scopes.

events.title: User Consents & Redirects Back
events.detail: The user logs in and approves permissions. The OAuth server redirects back to your redirect URI with a temporary authorization code.

events.title: Exchange Code for Tokens
events.detail: Your backend sends the authorization code and the original code_verifier to the token endpoint to prove identity.

events.title: Receive Access & ID Tokens
events.detail: The server validates the verifier and returns an Access Token, an ID Token, and optionally a Refresh Token.

blocks.note: This is the standard Authorization Code flow with PKCE, which is now the recommended best practice for both mobile and web apps.

exchanges.reqBody:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: oauth2.googleapis.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

code=4/0AdQt8q...&
client_id=your-client-id&
client_secret=your-client-secret&
redirect_uri=https://yourapp.com/callback&
exchanges.note: Your backend exchanges the short-lived authorization code for the actual access and ID tokens securely.

blocks.note: The token exchange happens entirely on your backend, keeping your client secret and the resulting tokens safe from the browser.

props.title: Session Cookies vs. JWTs

cells.value: Hard (Must wait for expiry or use a blacklist)
Minimal (Just a small session ID string)
XSS (If stored in LocalStorage, tokens can be stolen)

props.caption: How to keep users signed in after OAuth completes
props.footer: Use Session Cookies for standard web apps where instant revocation is critical. Use JWTs for APIs and microservices.

blocks.note: Cookies win on instant revocation and size, while JWTs win on statelessness and scalability across multiple microservices.

props.title: Token Storage Security Matrix

cells.reason: Any malicious script running on your page can read the tokens instantly.
Browsers don't automatically send LocalStorage values with requests.
Safer, but tokens are lost on page refresh, requiring silent refresh flows.
Not automatically attached to cross-site requests.
JavaScript cannot read HttpOnly cookies, blocking basic token theft.
Vulnerable to CSRF, but mitigated completely by using SameSite=Strict/Lax.

props.footer: Storing tokens in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie is the industry standard for web applications.

blocks.note: Never store sensitive access tokens in LocalStorage; an XSS vulnerability would allow an attacker to steal them instantly.

props.title: OAuth Implementation Threat Model

threats.mitigation: Use PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) to bind the code to the client.
Never expose the client secret in frontend code or mobile apps.
Validate JWT signatures using JWKS endpoints and verify the 'aud' and 'iss' claims.

props.footer: Ensure PKCE is enabled even for confidential server-side clients to prevent authorization code injection.

blocks.note: A robust threat model ensures you mitigate common OAuth pitfalls like code interception and client secret exposure.
